newsitem.title: UK: Brown moves into UK Treasury, faces tough decisions.
newsitem.headline: Brown moves into UK Treasury, faces tough decisions.

text.p: Gordon Brown arrived at Britain's Treasury early on Saturday for his first full day as Chancellor of the Exchequer and put interest rates and taxation at the top of a lengthy agenda.
A Treasury (finance ministry) spokeman said Brown had back-to-back meetings scheduled all day with senior officials.
Much of Saturday's discussion would focus on talks next Wednesday between the new Chancellor and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
Brown faces tough decisions in his first days in power, the first being whether to raise interest rates next week at a time when the the economy is precariously poised.

The new Labour government has inherited a booming economy combining low inflation and falling unemployment. But consumer demand is starting to overheat, the soaring pound is crippling exporters and public finances are still deeply in the red.
"Buoyant consumer demand, particularly in the service sector, will lead to rising inflation later this year," said Trevor Williams, chief economist at high street bank Lloyds TSB.

"But manufacturing growth is weak and lagging the rest of the economy. If interest rates are increased to slow domestic demand it could hit the wrong target and plunge manufacturing back into recession."
Manufacturers, already struggling to sell goods abroad because of the strong pound, fear another rate rise will send the currency even higher, making exports even more expensive.
But the Bank of England says inflationary pressures are building and an interest rate rise is urgently required.
Governor George is likely to advise Brown to push up the six percent interest rates by a quarter or even half a percentage point when he meets him on Wednesday.
It is a thorny dilemma for the new Chancellor.
Brown will win instant credibility in financial markets if he plumps for an early rate rise.
"If Brown really wants to be the iron Chancellor, it would be a help to start early," said Salomon Brothers economist Michael Saunders.
"If he delays, the markets are not going to be sure whether he's just waiting a month or if he's not going to be the iron chancellor after all."
But any decision to raise the cost of borrowing will be unpopular in the country, particularly among Britain's home owners who make up two thirds of all households.
Brown may delay a decision on interest rates until he has drawn up plans for the first budget, promised within two months.

Labour has promised one tax rise and one tax cut in the budget -- a windfall tax on privatised utilities to fund a "welfare-to-work" programme, and a cut in indirect tax (VAT) on heating fuel, to five percent from eight percent.
But independent economists say more is needed if the public finances are to improve and the consumer boom slowed.
"It would be a wasted opportunity if he only imposed the windfall tax and cut VAT on fuel," said Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets.
"Fiscal policy has to be tightening, whether in June 1997 or at the next budget in March next year."
Higher taxes on petrol would be popular with the environmental lobby, unpopular with motorists, but is an attractive option since the costs could be accommodated by falling world oil prices.
Alternatively, Brown could abolish tax relief on mortgages, calling that a palatable alternative to higher interest rates.
Financial market analysts say prices of British government bonds or gilts could improve if the government achieves a better balance between fiscal and monetary policy.
But the outlook for the pound and the stock market is more cloudy. If tax rises mean less need for interest rate rises, sterling will not like it.
The stock market will be nervous about the extent of the windfall tax and a likely reform of the corporation tax system.
